**The Weight of Light: A Meditation on Time, Memory, and the Unseen Forces That Shape Us**

---

### **I. The First Light**

There is a moment, fleeting as a breath between exhales, when the world is not yet a thing but a possibility. Before the first dawn, before the first name, before the first sorrow or joy—there is only the hum of the universe tuning itself, like a string plucked too softly to make sound. I wonder if that moment exists for anyone but the gods. Or perhaps it exists for all of us, buried deep in the quiet spaces between thoughts, where the mind is not yet a mind but a potential.

I was born in a city that did not know my name. Not yet. The doctors called me *patient*, the nurses called me *baby*, and my mother, in the first tremulous hours, called me *light*—not because I was bright, but because she had seen me in the way light bends through smoke, a fleeting shape that is almost there, almost real. She said it in a language I did not understand, but the sound of it—*luz*, *lumen*, *phos*—lingered in the air like the scent of rain on hot pavement. Light. Something that illuminates. Something that is gone before you can grasp it.

I did not know then that light is also the thing that burns. That it is the first and last thing we see, the thing that reveals and the thing that blinds. That it is the weight of the sun pressing down on the scales of our days, the thing that makes shadows stretch long and thin when we are afraid.

---

### **II. The Shape of Forgetting**

Memory is a river, but it does not flow. It is a series of still images, each one a snapshot of a moment that has already begun to fade before the camera clicks. I remember the taste of my grandmother’s *ají de gallina*—the way the spiced chicken melted on my tongue, the way the yuca starch thickened the sauce into something almost like memory itself. I remember the way her hands, rough from years of kneading dough and washing clothes, would press my cheek when she thought I wasn’t looking. I remember the smell of her perfume, something like jasmine and old paper, the scent of a life lived in books and stories.

But I do not remember her face. Not clearly. Only fragments: the curve of her smile, the way her eyes crinkled when she laughed, the silver threads in her hair that she would pull into a loose knot at the nape of her neck. The rest is a blur, a half-remembered dream. My mother says it is because I was too young. That children’s memories are like sand castles—built in the moment, washed away by the next tide.

I wonder if that is true. Or if forgetting is not the absence of memory, but the act of choosing what to hold onto. What to let go.

I think of the things I have forgotten: the exact sound of my father’s voice, the way the schoolyard smelled after rain, the name of the girl who sat beside me in third grade and whispered secrets about the stars. I think of the things I have tried to remember and failed—like the shape of my first love’s hands, the way her laugh sounded like wind chimes in a storm. Some memories are like that: beautiful, but just out of reach, like trying to catch a fish that slips through your fingers every time you think you have it.

And then there are the memories that refuse to let go. The ones that cling like barnacles to the hull of your soul. The night I saw my brother’s face in the mirror and realized he was not my brother at all, but a stranger who had taken his place. The way my mother’s voice cracked when she said his name. The way the world tilted sideways after that.

---

### **III. The Clockwork of Days**

Time is a thief. It steals not just years, but the very texture of our lives. It takes the sharp edges of youth and rounds them into something smooth and unremarkable. It turns our passions into habits, our dreams into routines, our fire into embers.

I have spent my life trying to outrun it. To freeze moments in time like butterflies in a glass case. I take photographs not because I want to remember, but because I want to *preserve*. I write letters I never send. I collect things—stones, shells, the occasional book with a dog-eared page—that I tell myself I will look at someday and feel something. But the someday never comes. The things gather dust. The feelings evaporate.

I think of the way clocks work. The way the hands move, inexorably, toward the next second, the next minute, the next hour. There is no stopping them. No going back. Only the relentless march forward, like a train that does not slow for passengers, only for the tracks.

I wonder if that is why we tell stories. Not just to remember, but to *resist*. To say, *This happened. This was important.* To carve our lives into the stone of time, so that even when we are gone, the shape remains.

---

### **IV. The Unseen Forces**

There are things that move in the world that we cannot see. Gravity, of course. But also the pull of habit, the weight of expectation, the invisible strings that connect us to the people we love and the people we hate. There is the force of memory, which drags us backward like a tide. There is the force of desire, which pulls us forward like a current. And there is the force of fear, which holds us still, like a hand clamped over our mouth.

I have spent my life trying to understand these forces. To map them, to name them, to find a way to live with them without being crushed.

I think of the way a magnet works. How it can lift a paperclip from across the room, how it can hold two pieces of metal together even when they are not touching. I think of how love is like that—an invisible force that binds us to someone else, even when we do not understand why. Even when we do not want to be bound.

I think of how hatred is like that too. How it can pull us apart, how it can make us see the world in black and white, in us and them. How it can turn a single moment—an insult, a glance, a word—into a chasm that we cannot cross.

I think of the way time is like that. How it can stretch a single day into an eternity of waiting, how it can compress a lifetime into the blink of an eye.

---

### **V. The Art of Letting Go**

There comes a moment in every life when you realize that you cannot hold onto everything. That some things must be released, like kites that have flown too high to be pulled back down. That some memories must be buried, like seeds in the earth, to make way for new growth.

I learned this the hard way. I spent years clinging to the past, to the things that had hurt me, to the people who had left me. I thought that if I held onto them tightly enough, they would not be able to escape. But they did. And in their absence, I realized that I had been holding my own life hostage.

I think of the way a river carves its path. It does not stop at the first obstacle. It does not turn back when the water is deep. It flows forward, reshaping the land around it, until it finds its way to the sea.

I think of the way a tree grows. It does not cling to the past. It does not fear the wind. It reaches upward, toward the light, and in doing so, it becomes something new.

I think of the way we must do the same.

---

### **VI. The Light That Remains**

There is a kind of light that does not come from the sun. It is the light of a candle in the dark. The light of a star on a clear night. The light of a person’s eyes when they are truly seen.

I have spent my life searching for this light. I have looked in the faces of strangers, in the pages of books, in the quiet corners of my own mind. And sometimes, I find it. Just for a moment. Just enough to know that it is there.

I think of the way a flame does not burn out. It only changes. It becomes something else—smoke, ash, memory. But the light remains, in the way the embers glow long after the fire is gone.

I think of the way we are like that. We do not burn out. We only change. We become something new. And in that becoming, we carry the light of what we were with us, like a secret we cannot forget.

---

### **VII. The Unfinished Story**

I do not know what will happen next. I do not know what the future holds. I do not even know what the present is, really, except as a fleeting moment that slips away before I can grasp it.

But I know this: that the world is full of light and shadow, of love and loss, of beauty and pain. That we are all, in some way, trying to make sense of it. That we are all, in some way, trying to hold onto the things that matter.

And I know this too: that some things cannot be held. That some things must be let go. That some lights must be allowed to go out, so that others can be lit.

I do not know what my story will be. But I know that it is not yet finished. That there are still pages to write, still words to say, still moments to live.

And so I will keep going. I will keep searching for the light. I will keep reaching for the stars.

Because that is what we do. That is what we are.

We reach.

We hope.

We live.

---

**Epilogue: The Shape of Now**

As I sit here, writing these words, the light outside is golden. The kind of light that comes just before sunset, when the world is soft and warm and full of possibility. I can see the shapes of trees, the way the sky bleeds into the earth, the way the air itself seems to hum with something unspoken.

I think of all the things I have written. Of all the things I have forgotten. Of all the things I have yet to say.

And I think of this moment. This *now*. This fleeting, precious, impossible-to-capture *now*.

I do not know what will come after. But for now, I am here. And that is enough.
